extracted.intended_audience: NSF program officers, MER co-directors, mathematics educators and program evaluators
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation criteria and methodological standards for assessing the Mathematicians and Education Reform Forum (MER), its individual and departmental components, and its contribution to systemic mathematics education reform. Includes program selection/eligibility rules, measures of individual and departmental impact, workshop design features, sustainability indicators, and evaluation methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: MER as a support mechanism (evaluation standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: MER functions more as a support mechanism for those members of the mathematics community already involved in educational efforts; therefore evaluating MER by whether it effectively supports these members is an appropriate standard of effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evaluators caution that attributing broad changes solely to MER is difficult because many participants were already involved in educational work before joining MER. Using 'supporting existing reformers' as the criterion avoids an unrealistically stringent test for voluntary networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual-level benefits / participant-reported outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure changes reported by individual participants: validation of personal experiences, acquisition of awareness of educational activities, enhanced personal teaching and/or research, feeling comfortable contacting MER colleagues, and self-reported changes in classroom pedagogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and observed metrics cited: ~60% of mathematicians and K-12 educators and 47% of math-educators said MER helped further their projects; >70% of mathematicians and K-12 educators and >50% of math-educators felt more aware of education issues; almost half of mathematicians reported changing their teaching (e.g., cooperative learning, technology adoption). Use surveys (closed- and open-ended) and interviews to quantify and exemplify these outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of positive departmental attitude change
rubrics_metrics.description: Departmental-level indicators include whether educational reform is valued and supported, and concrete signs such as improvements in curricula, attention to better pedagogy, and increased institutional support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported heuristics: over 50% felt reform was highly valued and ~75% felt it was at least accepted. Look for curricular adoption (e.g., reform calculus like Harvard Calculus), new entry-level or graduate courses on pedagogy, pre-service program rewrites, and administrative support programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental Network membership and commitment requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments joining MER's Departmental Network were required to demonstrate support for math education reform and to make an operational commitment (three-year commitment operationalized by sending teams to yearly workshops, maintaining MER Departmental E-Mail communication, and attempting to spread word within their departments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection was targeted to research universities considered role models; departments were invited based on co-directors' knowledge and Advisory Committee recommendations. Evaluate whether departments met the participation commitments (team attendance, e-mail engagement, internal outreach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application screening via departmental endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: The application process for individual workshops requires a letter of support from the applicant's department chair or dean to assure departmental backing and to serve as a screening mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is intended to provide up-front assurance of departmental support and to screen candidates. Assess whether letters reflect genuine departmental support (not merely formality) and whether this screening affects participant composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop quality and design
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of workshops measured by structure (overarching theme + breakouts), opportunities for informal contact (meals, social time), fostering interpersonal comfort, and follow-on collaborative initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departmental workshops were highlighted as especially effective; specific design elements to replicate or score include: clear theme, breakout sessions for specific interests, built-in informal time to build trust, and activities that seed collaborations (graduate exchanges, collaborative grants). Participant feedback and observed spontaneous initiatives are important evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of cross-departmental collaboration and concrete outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrable collaborative outputs that resulted from MER interactions, such as joint planning grants, interdisciplinary initiatives, graduate/postdoc exchanges, shared computer-based projects, or departmental surveys/databases to leverage resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate concrete follow-throughs (grant applications, enacted exchanges, created databases) and assess whether MER facilitated initiation, agreement among chairs, and persistence of these collaborations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of MER activity (K-14 vs postsecondary emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of MER's focus across educational levels: extent to which MER engages pre-college (K-12), first two years of undergraduate (K-14), and broader postsecondary reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report notes MER tended to focus on postsecondary issues where participants had most expertise despite stated pre-college emphasis; evaluate alignment between stated mission and actual activities and recommend improved coordination with K-12 organizations where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalization and sustainability (risk of dependence on few champions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether educational initiatives are institutionalized across departments or rest precariously on a few faculty; look for signs of sustainability (institutional support, rewarded efforts, presence of mathematics educators on faculty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include initiatives driven by one or two faculty whose departure causes efforts to falter (example: Penn State). Positive signs include distributed responsibility, formal institutional supports, and roles that outlast individual champions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership engagement (department chair involvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of leadership buy-in such as chair attendance at initial meetings and ongoing chair-level support, which increases the likelihood of broad departmental acceptance of MER activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report cites requesting chair attendance as a strategic move; loss of a chair liaison can weaken ties. Evaluate leadership continuity and active engagement as part of departmental commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication strategy and listserver moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of MER's intra-network communication practices, specifically the tradeoffs between restricting listserver subscription to a few liaisons (to avoid over-mailing) versus opening subscription to any interested individuals in departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider traffic volumes (low traffic reduces risk of flooding), moderation burdens on liaisons, and benefits of wider access for engagement. Evaluate whether current approach facilitates or inhibits information spread within departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between prescriptive and laissez-faire approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: MER should strike a balance between being too prescriptive (which might alienate potential mathematician participants) and too laissez-faire (which might accomplish little); success is measured by MER's ability to 'walk this fine line'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate participant receptivity and program uptake—does MER add ideas gently and gain traction without alienating its constituency?

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methodology standards (triangulation and mixed methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological criteria for evaluating MER: triangulate data sources (NSF officer, co-directors, workshops, advisory meetings, participants, documents, literature), use participant-observation, written questionnaires, interviews, site visits, document review, and both qualitative (coding/domain analysis) and quantitative (descriptive/inferential statistics) analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report details primary methods: surveying the entire population of ~730 participants (instead of sampling) due to inability to clearly stratify subpopulations, purposive case-site visits selected for maximal learning (best-case scenarios, geographic/programmatic representation), using a priori checklists plus responsive approaches, and interviewing a range of stakeholders (pro-, neutral-, anti-MER). Use these standards to judge evaluation rigor and representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and survey design justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify surveying the entire known participant population rather than probabilistic sampling when subpopulation identifiers are lacking and when minority subgroups (K-12 and math-educators) would be otherwise underrepresented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evaluators argued surveying all 730 past and current participants maximized chances of including smaller professional communities; document limitations (inability to stratify) and the tradeoffs inherent in a census-style survey approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case study site selection and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Select case study sites strategically (e.g., best-case institutions with active educational agendas) to learn about the network, ensure geographic and programmatic representation, and conduct intensive site visits including interviews with chairs, graduate students, pro/neutral/anti-MER faculty, and attendance at reformed classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-week site visits per institution, mixture of pre-ordinate checklist (documents, interviews) and responsive exploration; balance depth and representativeness and report reasons for purposive selection to contextualize findings.
